screens.title: Installing and Configuring MongoDB Community Edition
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how to install MongoDB Community Edition on a typical development machine, how the core processes work, and how to configure the server so it starts reliably. We'll cover the two critical programs you use every day: the database server, called mongod, and the interactive shell, mongosh. You will see concrete installation steps for Windows, Mac O S via Homebrew, and Debian/Ubuntu Linux using apt, plus how to create the data directory and where to look when things fail. This matters because a correct local setup is the foundation of hands-on learning and safe experimentation. As you follow the instructions, you will gain confidence starting the server, connecting to it, and checking its status. Keep an eye out for two common pitfalls I’ll highlight: forgetting to start mongod before connecting, and permission errors on the data directory. By the end of this chapter you will be able to start a MongoDB instance, open the shell to verify the server version, and edit a simple mongod. conf to change dbPath and logPath. Think about one project where having a local server will speed your iteration cycle — what will you build first?

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Installing and Configuring MongoDB Community Edition

This chapter teaches practical setup: installing the server, configuring storage and logs, running mongod as a service, and connecting with mongosh.

In this lesson
Install and start MongoDB on your OS and verify connectivity.
Key tools
Understand mongod (server) and mongosh (shell) roles.
Why it matters
A reliable local server speeds development and troubleshooting.
Quick orientation
  • mongod is the long-running database process that stores and serves data.
  • mongosh is the interactive shell you use to run queries and admin commands.
  • dbPath and logPath are configured in mongod.conf or via command-line flags.
Coming up: installation steps for Windows, macOS, and Linux, plus troubleshooting tips.
Visual concept
Connect the pieces
Server: mongod
Stores data, listens on port 27017 by default
Shell: mongosh
Interactive JavaScript interface for CRUD and admin
Config: mongod.conf
Defines dbPath, logPath, and network settings
Explore Key Topics
Install by OS
Windows MSI, Homebrew on macOS, apt on Debian/Ubuntu.
Run & Connect
Start mongod, then use mongosh to verify with db.version().
Configure paths
Set dbPath and logPath in mongod.conf or provide flags when launching.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you'll develop four core skills that make local MongoDB work for development. First, you'll install MongoDB Community Edition on a common operating system and confirm the server runs. For example, you'll follow the apt workflow on a Linux VM or use Homebrew on Mac O S, so you can replicate the environment later. Second, you'll identify and explain the roles of mongod and mongosh: mongod runs the database engine and mongosh is the interactive shell you use to query and administer that engine. Third, you'll configure basic server settings such as the data path and log path, using a simple mongod. conf so the server writes data where you expect and logs appear in a known file. Fourth, you will learn to start, stop, and connect to the server from the command line and troubleshoot common errors like permission issues or a refused connection. Each objective is tied to hands-on verification: create the data directory, start the server, run db. version() in mongosh, and inspect the log when something goes wrong. These skills matter because they turn conceptual knowledge into a dependable local workflow.

screens.title: What are mongod and mongosh?
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the two programs you will use constantly. mongod is the MongoDB daemon: the long-running process that manages data files, accepts client connections on a TCP port, and performs reads, writes, and internal data management. Think of mongod as the engine under the hood that keeps your data safe and answers queries. mongosh is the interactive JavaScript shell that connects to a running mongod instance. With mongosh you run commands, inspect databases and collections, and perform administration tasks. A concrete example: when you start mongod and then open mongosh, running db. version() in the shell returns the server version string provided by mongod; that proves the shell is connected and the engine is responding. A common misconception is to assume mongosh starts the server automatically — it does not. If mongod is not running, mongosh will show a connection error such as ECONNREFUSED. Another point of confusion is thinking mongod is only for production. In fact mongod is the same process you run locally for development; you simply control how it stores data and which network interfaces it listens on. Key takeaway: mongod provides the service, mongosh is your interactive client. Always ensure mongod is running before attempting shell commands.

keyIdea.title: mongod vs mongosh
keyIdea.text: mongod runs the database; mongosh is the interactive shell used to connect and operate the database.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › mongod & mongosh
Definition

mongod: database daemon

mongod is the primary server process that reads and writes data and listens for client connections on port 27017 by default. It manages storage, journaling, and networking.

Concrete example
Start mongod, then open the shell and run db.version() to verify the server responds with its version.
Definition

mongosh: interactive shell

mongosh is the JavaScript shell that connects to mongod for CRUD operations and administration. It does not start mongod; it only connects to it.

Command
mongosh
db.version()
Common mistake
Trying to run shell commands when mongod is not running causes a connection refused error; always start the server first.
Key Takeaway
mongod is the engine, mongosh is the steering wheel. Both are required for interactive work.

screens.title: Installation overview: Windows, macOS, Linux
screens.narratorSegment: Although the installer varies per operating system, the installation pattern is consistent: obtain the Community Edition package, install it so that mongod and mongosh are available, configure the service or background process, and verify connectivity. On Windows you typically use the MSI installer and choose to install MongoDB as a service so it starts on boot; you must then add the bin directory to the PATH so the commands are accessible from any prompt. On Mac O S the recommended path is Homebrew: tap the mongodb formula repository and install mongodb-community, then use brew services to run mongod as a background service. On Debian/Ubuntu Linux you import the MongoDB GPG key, add the repository to apt sources, run apt update, and install the mongodb-org package; systemd will usually control mongod as a service. The shared verification pattern is the same: ensure the data directory exists and is writable, start the server through the OS service manager or directly with mongod, then open mongosh and run db. version() to verify the connection. A common misconception is thinking the installer configures data and log directories for you in a way suitable for all workflows — always confirm the dbPath and logPath and change them if you need a custom location. The practical skill here is executing and verifying these four steps reliably across operating systems.

keyIdea.title: Shared install pattern
keyIdea.text: Obtain package → install → configure service → verify with mongosh and logs; check dbPath permissions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Install Overview
Process

Common installation steps

  1. Acquire the Community Edition package for your OS (MSI, Homebrew formula, or apt repo).
  2. Install so mongod and mongosh appear in the system path or bin directory.
  3. Decide whether to run mongod as a managed service or manually, and configure accordingly.
  4. Create and set permissions for the data directory, start the server, and verify with mongosh.
Example verification sequence: start mongod, run mongosh, then in the shell run db.version() to ensure the server responds.
Platform callouts
Windows (MSI)
Use the MSI installer, choose Custom to control the install location, and install as a service if you want automatic start on boot. Then add the bin folder to PATH.
macOS (Homebrew)
Use the Homebrew tap and the mongodb-community formula, then brew services start to run mongod in the background.
Linux (apt)
Import the GPG key, add the repository list file, apt update, and apt install mongodb-org. Use systemd commands to manage the service.
Common misconception: installers always choose safe defaults. Always confirm paths and permissions for your workflow.

screens.title: macOS installation with Homebrew
screens.narratorSegment: On Mac O S the recommended path in this chapter is Homebrew. Homebrew simplifies package management and will usually configure mongod to run as a service. The exact sequence is to tap the mongodb Homebrew repository and then install the mongodb-community@6.0 formula. After installation you can run brew services start mongodb-community@6.0 so the server runs in the background and restarts at login. A concrete example from the chapter is the two commands shown: first run the tap command to make the mongodb formulas available, then run brew install to fetch and install the package. A common error is attempting to start the service without Homebrew services installed or without sufficient privileges; verify brew services is available and that your user can run services. After starting, validate by running mongosh and then db. version() to confirm connectivity. If the server does not start, check Homebrew logs and the mongod log specified in the configuration. The practical result is a reproducible local server managed by Homebrew that you can stop, start, and upgrade with familiar package manager commands. macOS installation with Homebrew means tap the formula, install mongodb-community@6.0, then use brew services to run and manage mongod.. In practical terms, use homebrew to tap and install mongodb-community@6.0, then start the service. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Tap the formula, install mongodb-community@6.0, then use brew services to run and manage mongod.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › macOS Install
Commands
Run these exact Homebrew commands as shown in the chapter to install the Community Edition.
brew tap mongodb/brew
brew install mongodb-community@6.0
Run as a service
brew services start mongodb-community@6.0
brew services stop mongodb-community@6.0
Check logs if startup fails and confirm with mongosh.
Verify
Open a terminal and run mongosh; then in the shell run db.version() to confirm the server is reachable.
mongosh
> db.version()
Misconception: starting brew services guarantees no configuration change is needed. If you need a custom dbPath or logPath, create or edit mongod.conf and restart using that configuration.
Key Takeaway

Homebrew installs and manages mongod for easy start/stop and upgrades; always validate with the shell.

screens.title: Linux installation with apt (Debian/Ubuntu)
screens.narratorSegment: On Debian and Ubuntu systems the chapter walks through using the package manager to install MongoDB. The steps are intentional: import the MongoDB public GPG key so packages can be verified, add a repository list file tailored to your Ubuntu release, update package lists, and then install the mongodb-org package. The chapter provides the key commands for this flow. After installation, mongod is usually installed as a systemd service so you can start it and enable automatic startup with systemctl. For example, if mongod is not running you would start it with sudo systemctl start mongod and enable it at boot with sudo systemctl enable mongod. A common mistake is forgetting to replace the code name in the repository line with your distribution release; using the wrong release name can cause package resolution errors. Another frequent issue is permission errors on the default data directory; if /data/db is missing or unwritable, create it and set ownership so the mongod process can write data. The practical result is a system-managed MongoDB service that you can control with familiar service commands and that integrates with system logging and process supervision.

keyIdea.title: apt workflow
keyIdea.text: Import the GPG key, add the apt source list, apt update, apt install mongodb-org, then manage mongod with systemd.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Linux Install
Apt commands
Follow the sequence below to add MongoDB's repository and install the package.
wget -qO - https://www.mongodb.org/static/pgp/server-6.0.asc | sudo apt-key add -

echo "deb [ arch=amd64,arm64 ] https://repo.mongodb.org/apt/ubuntu focal/mongodb-org/6.0 multiverse" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/mongodb-org-6.0.list

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y mongodb-org
Replace 'focal' with your Ubuntu code name (for example 'jammy' for 22.04).
Service control
Once installed, manage mongod with systemctl.
sudo systemctl start mongod
sudo systemctl enable mongod
sudo systemctl status mongod
If you see connection refused when using mongosh, check whether mongod is active. If the service failed to start, inspect the logPath to find the root cause.
Common misconception: apt handles all configuration. Confirm dbPath and permissions yourself before trusting defaults.

screens.title: dbPath and logPath explained
screens.narratorSegment: Two configuration values are critical to a stable server: dbPath and logPath. The dbPath is the filesystem location where mongod stores database files. On Linux and Mac O S the chapter notes the common default of /data/db, and on Windows the default is C:\data\db. If this directory does not exist or mongod lacks write permission, the server will fail to start and will write clear errors to the log. The logPath is the file where mongod appends runtime messages; inspecting this file is the first step in most troubleshooting workflows. A practical configuration uses mongod. conf to set both values explicitly, for example pointing dbPath to /var/lib/mongodb and logPath to /var/log/mongodb/mongod. log. A common misconception is thinking files under /var or C:\Program Files are writable by a regular user — many default service accounts need specific ownership or privileges. The chapter guidance shows how to create the data directory and adjust ownership on Unix-like systems with mkdir and chown commands. The takeaway: set dbPath and logPath consciously, ensure permissions allow mongod to write, and consult the log when startup fails.

keyIdea.title: Storage & logs
keyIdea.text: dbPath holds database files; logPath holds runtime logs. Both must be set and writable by mongod.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › dbPath & logPath
Definition

dbPath: where data lives

dbPath points to the folder containing MongoDB's data files. Defaults vary by OS, but you should set and verify this path explicitly when possible.

Example commands from the chapter to prepare a Unix-like data directory:
sudo mkdir -p /data/db
sudo chown -R `id -un` /data/db
This gives your user ownership so mongod started by that user can write to the directory.
logPath: where logs go

Inspect logs to diagnose startup

A mongod.conf entry controls the log file location; check it when mongod fails to start or you see permission errors.

Example (from mongod.conf)
systemLog:
  destination: file
  path: /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log
  logAppend: true
Misconception: server logs are optional. In practice, log messages are your first and most reliable debugging signals when startup fails.

screens.title: Using mongod.conf to configure mongod
screens.narratorSegment: A configuration file gives you repeatable control over mongod's behavior. The chapter provides a minimal mongod. conf example that sets systemLog, storage, and network sections. For example, you can set the log destination to a file, give it a path, and enable logAppend so logs are appended across restarts. Under storage you set dbPath to the directory where data files should be kept. Under net you can change the port from the default 27017 and bind to specific interfaces; for local development binding to 127.0.0.1 is a good default to prevent external access. To start mongod with this file use mongod --config /etc/mongod. conf. A common misconception is that command-line flags and the config file are mutually exclusive; the config file provides persistent settings and flags can override them when needed. In practice, place the config file in a system location and use it for predictable behavior, especially when run as a service. After editing, restart the service so the new settings take effect and verify with mongosh. The takeaway: mongod. conf yields a declarative, auditable way to set dbPath, logPath, port, and bindIp.

keyIdea.title: Declarative config
keyIdea.text: mongod.conf provides a repeatable, auditable way to set dbPath, logPath, ports, and bind IPs; start mongod with --config to apply it.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › mongod.conf
Configuration
This minimal YAML config from the chapter sets file-based logging, a storage path, and network binding for local development.
# mongod.conf
systemLog:
  destination: file
  path: /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log
  logAppend: true
storage:
  dbPath: /var/lib/mongodb
net:
  port: 27017
  bindIp: 127.0.0.1
Start the server with: mongod --config /etc/mongod.conf. Use system service control when running as a managed service.
Practical notes
  • bindIp=127.0.0.1 prevents external connections — good for development.
  • Change dbPath and logPath to dedicated directories with proper permissions for production.
  • Flags can override config settings for temporary adjustments.
Key Takeaway

Use mongod.conf for repeatable, auditable server settings and restart mongod after edits.

screens.title: Start, stop, and connect: service commands and manual runs
screens.narratorSegment: Starting mongod can be done in two ways: as a managed system service or by running the mongod binary manually. When installed via package managers, mongod is commonly registered with the OS service manager. For example, on Linux use sudo systemctl start mongod and on Mac O S use brew services start mongodb-community@6.0. If you prefer to run mongod manually during development, pass the dbpath flag: mongod --dbpath /path/to/data. After starting the server, open a new terminal and run mongosh to connect. keyIdea.text: Manage mongod via system service or direct command; always verify with mongosh and consult logs on failure.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Run & Connect
Service commands
# Linux (systemd)
sudo systemctl start mongod
sudo systemctl enable mongod
sudo systemctl status mongod

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew services start mongodb-community@6.0
brew services stop mongodb-community@6.0
Use the service manager when you want automatic startup and integration with system logging.
Manual run
Run mongod directly to control the dbPath for quick experiments.
mongod --dbpath /path/to/your/data
mongod --config /etc/mongod.conf
Then open mongosh in a separate terminal and run db.version() to verify. If you see ECONNREFUSED, mongod is not listening; check the service or logs.
Pro tip: When debugging, use systemctl status and the log file referenced in mongod.conf to find the root cause quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to install MongoDB Community Edition on a typical development machine, how the core processes work, and how to configure the server so it starts reliably. We'll cover the two critical programs you use every day: the database server, called mongod, and the interactive shell, mongosh. You will see concrete installation steps for Windows, Mac O S via Homebrew, and Debian/Ubuntu Linux using apt, plus how to create the data directory and where to look when things fail. This matters because a correct local setup is the foundation of hands-on learning and safe experimentation. As you follow the instructions, you will gain confidence starting the server, connecting to it, and checking its status. Keep an eye out for two common pitfalls I’ll highlight: forgetting to start mongod before connecting, and permission errors on the data directory. By the end of this chapter you will be able to start a MongoDB instance, open the shell to verify the server version, and edit a simple mongod. conf to change dbPath and logPath. Think about one project where having a local server will speed your iteration cycle — what will you build first?

Over the next screens you'll develop four core skills that make local MongoDB work for development. First, you'll install MongoDB Community Edition on a common operating system and confirm the server runs. For example, you'll follow the apt workflow on a Linux VM or use Homebrew on Mac O S, so you can replicate the environment later. Second, you'll identify and explain the roles of mongod and mongosh: mongod runs the database engine and mongosh is the interactive shell you use to query and administer that engine. Third, you'll configure basic server settings such as the data path and log path, using a simple mongod. conf so the server writes data where you expect and logs appear in a known file. Fourth, you will learn to start, stop, and connect to the server from the command line and troubleshoot common errors like permission issues or a refused connection. Each objective is tied to hands-on verification: create the data directory, start the server, run db. version() in mongosh, and inspect the log when something goes wrong. These skills matter because they turn conceptual knowledge into a dependable local workflow.

This second objectives screen zooms into the hands-on tasks you will complete in the lab. You will create or verify the data directory used by mongod, and set correct filesystem permissions so the server can write data. You will practice starting and stopping mongod as a system service or background process depending on your operating system, and then connect using mongosh to run db. version() to prove the server is responsive. You will also edit a minimal mongod. conf to change dbPath and logPath and restart the server using that configuration. Finally, you will interpret common error messages like permission denied or connection refused by checking the mongod logs and service status. These tasks are small but essential: they teach you how to validate the installation and how to diagnose the most common setup problems quickly. When you finish, try to reproduce the same steps on another machine or a VM to confirm repeatability.

Let's define the two programs you will use constantly. mongod is the MongoDB daemon: the long-running process that manages data files, accepts client connections on a TCP port, and performs reads, writes, and internal data management. Think of mongod as the engine under the hood that keeps your data safe and answers queries. mongosh is the interactive JavaScript shell that connects to a running mongod instance. With mongosh you run commands, inspect databases and collections, and perform administration tasks. A concrete example: when you start mongod and then open mongosh, running db. version() in the shell returns the server version string provided by mongod; that proves the shell is connected and the engine is responding. A common misconception is to assume mongosh starts the server automatically — it does not. If mongod is not running, mongosh will show a connection error such as ECONNREFUSED. Another point of confusion is thinking mongod is only for production. In fact mongod is the same process you run locally for development; you simply control how it stores data and which network interfaces it listens on. Key takeaway: mongod provides the service, mongosh is your interactive client. Always ensure mongod is running before attempting shell commands.

Although the installer varies per operating system, the installation pattern is consistent: obtain the Community Edition package, install it so that mongod and mongosh are available, configure the service or background process, and verify connectivity. On Windows you typically use the MSI installer and choose to install MongoDB as a service so it starts on boot; you must then add the bin directory to the PATH so the commands are accessible from any prompt. On Mac O S the recommended path is Homebrew: tap the mongodb formula repository and install mongodb-community, then use brew services to run mongod as a background service. On Debian/Ubuntu Linux you import the MongoDB GPG key, add the repository to apt sources, run apt update, and install the mongodb-org package; systemd will usually control mongod as a service. The shared verification pattern is the same: ensure the data directory exists and is writable, start the server through the OS service manager or directly with mongod, then open mongosh and run db. version() to verify the connection. A common misconception is thinking the installer configures data and log directories for you in a way suitable for all workflows — always confirm the dbPath and logPath and change them if you need a custom location. The practical skill here is executing and verifying these four steps reliably across operating systems.

On Mac O S the recommended path in this chapter is Homebrew. Homebrew simplifies package management and will usually configure mongod to run as a service. The exact sequence is to tap the mongodb Homebrew repository and then install the mongodb-community@6.0 formula. After installation you can run brew services start mongodb-community@6.0 so the server runs in the background and restarts at login. A concrete example from the chapter is the two commands shown: first run the tap command to make the mongodb formulas available, then run brew install to fetch and install the package. A common error is attempting to start the service without Homebrew services installed or without sufficient privileges; verify brew services is available and that your user can run services. After starting, validate by running mongosh and then db. version() to confirm connectivity. If the server does not start, check Homebrew logs and the mongod log specified in the configuration. The practical result is a reproducible local server managed by Homebrew that you can stop, start, and upgrade with familiar package manager commands. macOS installation with Homebrew means tap the formula, install mongodb-community@6.0, then use brew services to run and manage mongod.. In practical terms, use homebrew to tap and install mongodb-community@6.0, then start the service. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

On Debian and Ubuntu systems the chapter walks through using the package manager to install MongoDB. The steps are intentional: import the MongoDB public GPG key so packages can be verified, add a repository list file tailored to your Ubuntu release, update package lists, and then install the mongodb-org package. The chapter provides the key commands for this flow. After installation, mongod is usually installed as a systemd service so you can start it and enable automatic startup with systemctl. For example, if mongod is not running you would start it with sudo systemctl start mongod and enable it at boot with sudo systemctl enable mongod. A common mistake is forgetting to replace the code name in the repository line with your distribution release; using the wrong release name can cause package resolution errors. Another frequent issue is permission errors on the default data directory; if /data/db is missing or unwritable, create it and set ownership so the mongod process can write data. The practical result is a system-managed MongoDB service that you can control with familiar service commands and that integrates with system logging and process supervision.

Two configuration values are critical to a stable server: dbPath and logPath. The dbPath is the filesystem location where mongod stores database files. On Linux and Mac O S the chapter notes the common default of /data/db, and on Windows the default is C:\data\db. If this directory does not exist or mongod lacks write permission, the server will fail to start and will write clear errors to the log. The logPath is the file where mongod appends runtime messages; inspecting this file is the first step in most troubleshooting workflows. A practical configuration uses mongod. conf to set both values explicitly, for example pointing dbPath to /var/lib/mongodb and logPath to /var/log/mongodb/mongod. log. A common misconception is thinking files under /var or C:\Program Files are writable by a regular user — many default service accounts need specific ownership or privileges. The chapter guidance shows how to create the data directory and adjust ownership on Unix-like systems with mkdir and chown commands. The takeaway: set dbPath and logPath consciously, ensure permissions allow mongod to write, and consult the log when startup fails.

A configuration file gives you repeatable control over mongod's behavior. The chapter provides a minimal mongod. conf example that sets systemLog, storage, and network sections. For example, you can set the log destination to a file, give it a path, and enable logAppend so logs are appended across restarts. Under storage you set dbPath to the directory where data files should be kept. Under net you can change the port from the default 27017 and bind to specific interfaces; for local development binding to 127.0.0.1 is a good default to prevent external access. To start mongod with this file use mongod --config /etc/mongod. conf. A common misconception is that command-line flags and the config file are mutually exclusive; the config file provides persistent settings and flags can override them when needed. In practice, place the config file in a system location and use it for predictable behavior, especially when run as a service. After editing, restart the service so the new settings take effect and verify with mongosh. The takeaway: mongod. conf yields a declarative, auditable way to set dbPath, logPath, port, and bindIp.
